passA.summary: Alex Volkov stages a debate between two AI Engineer Europe talks — Ryan LeFebvre's "code is free" optimism and Mario Zechner's "read every effing line" caution — and argues both are right about different things. He walks through 2026 data (Faros AI's 22,000-engineer survey, Anthropic's own numbers) showing that AI-assisted output has genuinely exploded while stability has not: code deletion per PR up 861%, but incidents per PR up 242% and bugs per developer up 6x. His mea culpa is that the continuum he coined is not a spectrum of engineers but of tasks: authentication, money movement, permissions, and irreversible data get line-by-line review, while non-critical code can be routed to systemic proof (linters, docs, evals, traces, shadow mode) instead of human eyes. He closes on "capability drift" — as models improve, the review layer moves up from outputs to task direction to loops, but the requirement for proof never disappears, and self-grading agent loops hide review rather than remove it. Worth watching if you manage engineers arguing about this in Slack; the routing table slide is the practical artifact.
key_points: The framing question "should I still read code in 2026?" is the wrong one; the better question is "what proof does this specific change need?", since the same engineer should YOLO some tasks and read every line of others.

The optimists are empirically right about output: the Faros AI April 2026 survey of 22,000 engineers shows an 861% increase in code deletion per PR, and Anthropic reports shipping eight times more code per quarter than in 2025.

The pessimists are empirically right about stability: the same survey shows a 242% increase in incidents per PR, a 31% increase in PRs merged with no review at all (human or agentic), and bugs per developer up six times over 2025.
Volkov's routing table says to read every line for authentication, money movement, permissions, and irreversible data, and to route everything else to systemic proof.

LeFebvre and Zechner agree more than their framings suggest: LeFebvre's mechanism is moving attention up a layer (encode the caught mistake into docs, linters, and reviewers so the system remembers), while Zechner's is routing by criticality.
Separating the agent that writes code from the agent that reviews and tests it is essential — otherwise it's like writing your own exam, taking it, and grading yourself.
Anthropic's own RSI essay predicts 10x-to-1000x output growth and names human code review as the new bottleneck via Amdahl's law, yet neither Anthropic nor OpenAI is removing humans from the loop.
Loops — scheduled agents that discover a task, write the plan, execute, and verify themselves — are the emerging primitive, but a builder that grades itself hasn't removed the review, only hidden it.

Capability drift moves where proof belongs (outputs → task direction → loops) but never removes the requirement for proof, which is why flexibility, not a fixed practice, is what keeps you an engineer.

notable_quotes.text: Because code got cheap, attention didn't.
notable_quotes.why: The talk's thesis compressed into one line.

notable_quotes.text: In fact, 80% of Anthropic's code is now AI written and this is this stat is at least a few months old.
notable_quotes.why: Concrete number anchoring the claim that hand-written code is now the exception at frontier labs.

notable_quotes.text: They're seeing 14x the number of commits, which is insane and most of this is AI assisted.
notable_quotes.why: Quantifies the industry-wide output explosion via GitHub.

notable_quotes.text: It's free for you to produce, free to refactor, and it is not a thing to get hung up on anymore. Humans no longer need to concern themselves with implementation.
notable_quotes.why: The maximalist pole of the continuum, in LeFebvre's own words.

notable_quotes.text: The important thing is not the code, but the prompt and the guardrails that got you there.
notable_quotes.why: States where the optimist camp thinks attention should move.

notable_quotes.text: Agents are actually compounding booboos, which is my word for errors, with zero learning and no bottlenecks and delayed pain.
notable_quotes.why: Zechner's mechanism for why unreviewed agent output degrades over time.

notable_quotes.text: Non-critical code, sure, write slop ahead. Critical code, read every line.
notable_quotes.why: The cautious pole, and already a task-routing rule rather than a blanket one.

notable_quotes.text: 861% increase in code deletion per PR. So us together with AI agents, we love deleting code.
notable_quotes.why: Headline stat from the Faros AI survey supporting the optimists.

notable_quotes.text: Anthropic also said that they're shipping eight times more code per quarter than in 2025.
notable_quotes.why: Reported throughput figure from the company with the most AI-generated code.

notable_quotes.text: Same essay, 31% increase in PRs merged with no review at all, human or agentic. Don't do this. I beg of you.
notable_quotes.why: The one practice Volkov flatly condemns, with a number attached.

notable_quotes.text: Same study, 242% increase in incident per PR. This kind of scary. The second study is also scary. Bugs per developer is up six times than 2025.
notable_quotes.why: The counterweight data showing output gains are not free.

notable_quotes.text: The continuum is real. It's not about the people. It's about the task.
notable_quotes.why: The talk's central correction and reusable reframe.

notable_quotes.text: He's not saying don't inspect your code. He's saying inspect the system, not every line.
notable_quotes.why: Reconciles the two poles by distinguishing object-level from system-level review.

notable_quotes.text: I think the better question right now for all of us is what proof does this specific change need?
notable_quotes.why: Replaces the binary question with the operational one.

notable_quotes.text: You read every line of authentication, money movement, permissions, and irreversible data.
notable_quotes.why: The concrete, checkable boundary of the routing table.

notable_quotes.text: This is what Ryan Le Popo talks about. Build the system that builds the system because read spends your attention once, engineer makes the system remember.
notable_quotes.why: Names the tradeoff between one-time attention and durable systemic proof.

notable_quotes.text: We used to check if Claude is doing the work right. With Fable, we check if Claude is doing the right work.
notable_quotes.why: Captures the capability-driven shift in what review is even for.

notable_quotes.text: It's never felt so tempting to stop looking at code at all. But don't do this in production.
notable_quotes.why: Karpathy stating the anxiety from both ends in one sentence.

notable_quotes.text: Capability drift changes where proof belongs. It doesn't remove the requirement of proof.
notable_quotes.why: The talk's answer to "does this survive the next model?"

notable_quotes.text: But if the builder grades itself, you didn't remove the review, you hid it.
notable_quotes.why: The sharpest critique of self-verifying agent loops.

notable_quotes.text: So again, loops don't remove judgment, but they do raise the stakes on where you put it.
notable_quotes.why: Positions loops as an amplifier of review placement, not a replacement.

notable_quotes.text: Not every line in 2026 needs your eyes. Every system still needs your judgment.
notable_quotes.why: The closing formulation of the whole argument.

guardrails and linting as systemic proof

positions.claim: The read-every-line vs. code-is-free continuum is a property of tasks, not of engineers; the same engineer should sit at both ends depending on the change.
Authentication, money movement, permissions, and irreversible data changes must be read line by line by a human.
Merging PRs with no review at all — human or agentic — is unacceptable practice, and it rose 31% per the Faros AI survey.
AI-driven output gains are real but come with a stability cost: 242% more incidents per PR and 6x more bugs per developer than 2025.
The same agent should not both write the code and write/grade its tests, because self-scoring is not productive verification.
Self-verifying loops do not eliminate review; they conceal it, and relying entirely on them degrades product quality.
Rising model capability relocates where proof is required but never removes the requirement for proof.
LeFebvre and Zechner are not actually in opposition — one advocates inspecting the system rather than every line, the other advocates routing by criticality.
Encoding a caught mistake into documentation, linters, and reviewers is more durable than catching it again in review, because humans are unreliable at catching repeated mistakes of the same type.
Advice from lab engineers about loops should be treated as a lighthouse rather than immediate practice, because their tokens are free and yours are not.
Anthropic's status page instability is suggestive evidence that high AI-generated code output does not imply stability.
Agents are better than humans at decomposing large changes into atomic reviewable PRs, and should be asked to do so.
